515.content:
Volume-based pricing changes the charge according to the quantity of service delivered. The volume may be users, storage, bandwidth, processing power, transaction rate, or another measured capacity.

The contract must define precisely whether it counts allocated, average, peak, or concurrent volume. Because demand changes over business cycles and events, both measurement and reporting determine whether the model remains fair and predictable.

518.title: Volume Unit Scaling
518.heading: Volume Unit Scaling
518.content: A cubic unit contains three powers of length, so a length-scale change must affect volume by the cube of that ratio. Pryor's conversion table includes cubic feet, cubic meters, liters, and acre-feet; his acre-foot example first reaches cubic meters and then liters. This two-step route makes clear that a unit may encode a special area-times-length construction while still describing volume. Writing $\mathrm{m^3}$ or L explicitly helps detect a mistaken area or length factor. Liquid and dry variants also require the right [[Unit Name Qualifiers in Conversion Tables|unit-name qualifier]]. See [[Area Unit Scaling]] and [[Volumetric Flow Rate Conversion]].

521.title: Volume Specification
521.heading: Volume Specification
521.content:
Volume specification defines a bounded three-dimensional region associated with a physical object or space. The user may indicate corners, faces, an axis, or another small set of constraints from which the system constructs a box, cylinder, or related primitive.

Using a constrained primitive reduces the number of difficult spatial inputs. The volume can support selection, collision, annotation, occlusion, or a starting approximation for more detailed reconstruction.

524.title: Volcano Plot
524.heading: Volcano Plot
524.content:
A volcano plot displays an effect estimate on the horizontal axis and negative log p-value on the vertical axis for many tested features. Large effects appear far from the center, while small p-values appear high on the graph.

The display prevents significance from being viewed without magnitude and can expose asymmetry or unusual groups of features. It does not correct for multiple testing; thresholds and q-values must be interpreted separately.

527.title: Visual Word Clustering
527.heading: Visual Word Clustering
527.content:
A visual-word representation quantizes local image descriptors into a learned codebook and describes an image by the frequency or arrangement of codewords. This converts variable sets of local features into vectors suitable for clustering.

Codebook size controls the tradeoff between discrimination and robustness. Quantization can discard spatial relationships and make visually distinct patches share a word, so extensions add spatial layout or soft assignments.

530.sourceSearchName: voice user interface voice user interface
530.title: Voice User Interface
530.heading: Voice User Interface
530.content:
A voice user interface lets people control a system through speech and hear or see its responses. Its design includes prompts, vocabulary, turn-taking, error recovery, and expectations about what the assistant can do.

Careful VUI design can compensate for imperfect [[Automatic Speech Recognition]] by narrowing likely answers with a [[Directed Prompt]], confirming risky choices, and giving users a clear path after a mismatch.

533.title: Visualization Registration
533.heading: Visualization Registration
533.content:
Visualization registration determines the physical frame to which displayed information is attached. A locally registered visualization follows a nearby object or surface, while a globally registered one is positioned within a larger world coordinate system.

The choice communicates meaning: a label attached to a machine part expresses a different relationship from an overview fixed to the room. Tracking and calibration error must be judged relative to the scale and task of that relationship.

536.title: Visual Shape
536.heading: Visual Shape
536.content:
Visual shape is the representational meaning created by arranging ordinary game objects into a recognizable larger form. A collection of walls, gates, and water can read as a castle and moat, giving the player context for the obstacle and its goal.

This differs from [[Scene Shape]], which describes the structure of choices over time. The two can reinforce each other when the image formed by a scene suggests how the player should interpret and navigate its possibilities.

538.title: Visual Scripting
538.heading: Document

2026-09-18 17:13

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Scripting and Data Formats]]

539.title: Visual Scripting
539.heading: Visual Scripting
539.content:
Visual scripting represents operations, values, and control flow as graphical elements and connections. It lets authors assemble behavior without writing the equivalent textual syntax directly.

The visual form still defines a program that must be validated and executed. It can make local flow approachable, but large graphs need organization and abstraction so connections do not become harder to understand than text.

542.title: Visual Motif
542.heading: Visual Motif
542.content:
A visual motif is a recurring shape, color, material, or image that represents a consistent rule or class of objects. Once the player learns one instance, later appearances can communicate their likely function without explicit instruction.

Motifs form a visual vocabulary and shape expectations. A motif can also develop by preserving its core meaning while appearing in new interactions, but inconsistent use risks visual miscommunication.

544.sourceSearchName: visual feature representation visual feature representation
544.title: Visual Feature Representation
544.heading: Document

545.sourceSearchName: visual feature representation visual feature representation
545.title: Visual Feature Representation
545.heading: Visual Feature Representation
545.content:
Visual feature representation converts an image or region into measurements that a learning algorithm can compare. A representation may be engineered from color, texture, and shape, or learned as a latent feature space from image data.

The choice determines which distinctions become easy for a model to detect. Handcrafted descriptors expose a defined visual property, while dimension-reduction and deep methods trade some direct interpretation for compact or task-adapted representations.

546.title: Visual Feature Representation

547.title: Visual Clustering Steering
547.heading: Document

548.sourceSearchName: visual clustering steering visual clustering steering
548.title: Visual Clustering Steering
548.heading: Visual Clustering Steering
548.content:
Visual clustering steering presents projections, cluster summaries, and uncertain boundaries through which an analyst can guide the search. Actions such as selecting a region, merging groups, or adjusting emphasis are translated into model updates.

The visualization must preserve enough structure for decisions to be informed rather than decorative. Projection distortion can make separated points look close or conceal overlap, so coordinated quantitative diagnostics remain important.

549.sourceSearchName: visual clustering steering visual clustering steering
549.title: Visual Clustering Steering
549.heading: References

551.title: Visual Display
551.heading: Visual Display
551.content:
A visual display is an [[Output Device]] that presents information through the human visual system. In a [[3D User Interface]], real-time graphics produce images that the device turns into perceptible light.

Important characteristics include [[Field of View]], [[Field of Regard]], [[Spatial Resolution]], screen geometry, light-transfer method, [[Refresh Rate]], ergonomics, and support for [[Depth Cue]]s. These characteristics interact with the task and technique. A front-projected screen, for example, can make direct manipulation difficult when the user's hand casts a shadow, while a wide display can make better use of peripheral vision.

An AR display can combine real and generated imagery through [[Optical See-Through Display|optical see-through]], [[Video See-Through Display|video see-through]], or [[Spatial Augmented Reality|spatial projection]]. These methods give the system different control over occlusion, brightness, focus, viewpoint, and the real image itself, so no one arrangement satisfies every application.

554.heading: Visual Discrimination in Time-Series Groups
554.content: Visual discrimination in time-series groups is the ability to distinguish multiple trajectories reliably through color, line, label, or panel arrangement. A qualitative palette must contain separable colors, but an arbitrary palette does not express similarity. The source orders colors using hierarchical clustering of temporal behavior so visually related trajectories receive related hues. [[Direct Time-Series Labeling]] can reduce dependence on color when the number of groups exceeds comfortable legend use.

557.title: Visual Coherence
557.heading: Visual Coherence
557.content:
Visual coherence is the perceptual agreement that makes real and virtual parts of an augmented image appear to occupy one scene. Position, depth ordering, illumination, image formation, and style must provide compatible evidence rather than revealing two unrelated layers.

The AR rendering pipeline acquires a model of the real scene, establishes geometric and photometric registration, composites real and virtual imagery, and presents the result. Errors in any stage can break the apparent relationship.

560.title: Visual Classification
560.heading: Visual Classification
560.content:
Visual classification joins interactive visualization with model construction or prediction so that a person can inspect data, boundaries, features, and uncertain cases. The display acts as a reasoning interface rather than a decorative report.

Useful systems must represent high-dimensional evidence without overwhelming the viewer and must connect visible actions to reproducible classifier changes. Human feedback can then supplement labels or model constraints.

563.title: VisiCalc
563.heading: VisiCalc
563.content:
VisiCalc was an early electronic spreadsheet whose interactive grid let users change a value and immediately see related calculations update. It gave the Apple II a compelling business purpose.

The program put financial modeling under direct user control in a way batch mainframes could not match. It became an example of application software driving demand for a hardware platform.

566.title: Viscous Flow
566.heading: Viscous Flow
566.content:
Viscous flow retains nonzero fluid viscosity and the relationship between shear stress and deformation rate. It can develop boundary layers and frictional losses that an inviscid model omits.

The primer contrasts this regime with its ideal potential-flow examples. Choosing a viscous or inviscid formulation changes the governing equations, element variables, and necessary boundary conditions.

569.title: Vis-Viva Orbital Energy Relation
569.heading: Vis-Viva Orbital Energy Relation
569.content: The vis-viva relation gives orbital speed from the current radius and the orbit's semi-major axis. It follows from conservation of mechanical energy and applies to elliptical motion, where speed is greatest near periapsis and lowest near apoapsis. Circular-orbit speed appears when the current radius equals the semi-major axis.

571.heading: Document

572.sourceSearchName: virus component model virus component model
572.title: Virus Component Model
572.heading: Virus Component Model
572.content:
The virus component model separates a [[Computer Virus]] into an infection mechanism, a trigger, and a payload. The infection mechanism finds and modifies hosts, the trigger determines when another behavior begins, and the payload performs the intended effect.

This decomposition prevents replication from being mistaken for the virus's objective. Two viruses can use similar infection methods while carrying very different triggers and payloads, or share an effect while spreading differently.

575.title: Virtual Reality
575.heading: Virtual Reality
575.content:
Virtual reality is an approach that uses displays, [[3D Tracking]], and other technologies to immerse a user in a [[Virtual Environment]]. It replaces the person's view of the physical environment with a synthetic spatial world and can create [[Presence]], the feeling of being there.

Immersion does not guarantee a usable experience. The [[3D User Interface]] must coordinate input, output, interaction techniques, and human capabilities. Inconsistent sensory information, poor ergonomics, or excessive [[Latency]] can reduce performance and contribute to [[Cybersickness]].

Unlike [[Augmented Reality]], which keeps the physical world as the main setting and attaches virtual information to it, VR makes the generated environment the user's primary visible world. The two can still share stereoscopic displays, viewpoint tracking, spatial interaction, and rendering techniques.

577.title: Virtual Private Network

578.sourceSearchName: virtual private network virtual private network
578.title: Virtual Private Network
578.heading: Virtual Private Network
578.content:
A virtual private network creates an [[Encrypted Communication Channel]] across a network that is not itself trusted. It can protect [[Data in Transit]] and give a remote device logical access to resources as though it were connected through a controlled network boundary.

A VPN protects the tunnel, not every endpoint or application using it. Identity checks, device security, access limits, and monitoring remain necessary parts of [[Defense in Depth]].

581.sourceSearchName: virtual memory protection virtual memory protection
581.title: Virtual Memory Protection
581.heading: Virtual Memory Protection
581.content:
Virtual memory gives each process a controlled address space that the operating system maps onto physical memory. The mapping can isolate process pages and attach permissions that distinguish readable, writable, or executable regions.

Because processes work through virtual rather than unrestricted physical addresses, one process cannot ordinarily name another process's memory directly. The mechanism contributes to [[Memory Protection]] alongside process isolation and hardware enforcement.

584.title: Virtual Machine
584.heading: Virtual Machine
584.content:
A virtual machine is a software-defined computer instance that runs on shared physical hardware. It presents processors, memory, storage, and networking to its own operating system while remaining logically separate from other virtual machines on the host.

Cloud resource pools can create or remove virtual machines to alter capacity quickly. This makes the virtual machine an important unit for [[Server Virtualization]], [[Horizontal Scalability]], and infrastructure delivery.

587.title: Virtual Environment
587.heading: Virtual Environment
587.content:
A virtual environment is a synthetic spatial world, usually three-dimensional, seen from a first-person point of view. The user's view is controlled in real time.

A virtual environment is the world being experienced, while [[Virtual Reality]] is an approach that uses displays, tracking, and other technologies to immerse a person in that world. The terms are often used interchangeably in practice.

Interaction within a virtual environment can involve [[3D Manipulation]], [[Navigation]], and [[System Control]], supported by a [[3D User Interface]].

590.heading: Virtual Machine Power Metering
590.content:
Virtual machine power metering estimates the share of a physical server's consumption attributable to each virtual machine. It combines host-level measurements with monitored CPU, memory, storage, and network activity.

The estimate can support energy-aware billing and scheduling, although shared components make exact attribution difficult. A model must state how it divides static power and interference among tenants.

593.heading: Virtual Machine Migration
593.content:
Virtual machine migration transfers a running or paused machine's memory, device, and execution state from one host to another. It preserves a workload when a host must leave, undergo maintenance, or rebalance capacity.

In a vehicular cloud, migration must complete before the vehicle departs; dirty memory rate, image size, network bandwidth, and destination readiness determine whether that is feasible.

596.title: Virtual Destructor in Algorithm Hierarchies
596.heading: Virtual Destructor in Algorithm Hierarchies
596.content:
A virtual destructor ensures that deleting an object through a base pointer invokes the derived destructor before the base destructor. ClusLib gives base classes such as Algorithm, Distance, Cluster, Schema, and Node virtual destructors when they participate in runtime polymorphism.

Without this rule, derived resources may not be released and behavior is undefined. Declaring the destructor virtual documents that the class is intended as a polymorphic boundary even when the base itself owns little state.

599.title: Virtual Assistant
599.heading: Virtual Assistant
599.content:
A virtual assistant is a software system that accepts natural-language requests, interprets what the user wants, and returns information or performs an action. Its conversational surface should not be confused with intelligence: a fluent response can hide a narrow service, while a constrained [[Voice User Interface]] can expose a capable one.

A complete assistant commonly combines [[Automatic Speech Recognition]], [[Natural Language Understanding]], a [[Dialog Manager]], [[Natural Language Generation]], [[Text-to-Speech]], and [[Digital Service Integration]].

601.title: Virtual Assistant Pipeline
601.heading: Document

602.sourceSearchName: virtual assistant pipeline virtual assistant pipeline
602.title: Virtual Assistant Pipeline
602.heading: Virtual Assistant Pipeline
602.content:
A virtual assistant pipeline transforms a user's signal through a sequence of specialized modules. Audio passes from conversion and [[Automatic Speech Recognition]] to [[Natural Language Understanding]] and a [[Dialog Manager]], after which [[Natural Language Generation]] and [[Text-to-Speech]] can produce a spoken reply.

The pipeline is also connected to external services that supply information or carry out actions. Its modular form allows individual components to be improved while keeping their input and output contracts stable.

605.sourceSearchName: virtual and potential temperature virtual and potential temperature
605.title: Virtual and Potential Temperature
605.heading: Virtual and Potential Temperature
605.content: Virtual temperature is the temperature dry air would need in order to have the same pressure and density as a parcel of moist air. Potential temperature is the temperature a parcel would reach if brought adiabatically to a reference pressure of 1,000 millibars. These transformations make air parcels comparable despite differences in moisture or pressure and support analysis of [[Atmospheric Lapse Rates and Stability]].

606.title: Virtual and Potential Temperature

608.title: Virtual Agent
608.heading: Virtual Agent
608.content:
A virtual agent is an assistant designed to represent an organization in a bounded service interaction. It typically guides users through tasks such as customer support, reservations, or account operations rather than offering the broad capabilities of a [[Personal Virtual Assistant]].

Because its domain is narrow, a virtual agent can use [[Directed Dialog]] and a controlled [[Voice User Interface]] to reduce ambiguity and recover from recognition or understanding errors.

611.title: Violin Plot
611.heading: Violin Plot
611.content:
A violin plot mirrors a smoothed density estimate around a categorical position to show the shape of a continuous distribution. It can reveal skewness or multiple modes hidden by a [[Box Plot]].

Its width represents estimated density rather than sample size unless explicitly scaled, so the bandwidth and accompanying summaries matter.

614.title: Vignetting
614.heading: Vignetting
614.content:
Vignetting is the reduction of image brightness toward the edges of a camera image. It can arise from the lens and camera geometry even when the physical scene has uniform illumination.

If ideal virtual pixels are composited over a vignetted image, their edge brightness can reveal the overlay. Measuring or modeling the falloff and applying it to the generated imagery improves photometric agreement.

617.title: Viewpoint Offset
617.heading: Viewpoint Offset
617.content:
Viewpoint offset is the displacement between the viewpoint that captures or generates an image and the eye position from which the user interprets it. In handheld and video see-through systems, the camera is commonly located away from the user's actual eye.

Nearby geometry makes the discrepancy especially noticeable because perspective changes rapidly with viewpoint. Image warping can compensate when sufficient scene geometry is known, but otherwise the offset can distort spatial judgments and hand-eye coordination.

620.title: Viewpoint Guidance
620.heading: Viewpoint Guidance
620.content:
Viewpoint guidance gives perceptual cues that help a user move or aim the display toward a useful view. The target may be an off-screen object, a physical location, or a particular camera pose required to inspect or capture something.

Arrows, frames, paths, and changing visual indicators can encode direction and remaining difference. Feedback should distinguish translation from rotation and remain interpretable while the target is outside the current field of view.

622.sourceSearchName: video mediated collaboration video mediated collaboration
622.title: Video-Mediated Collaboration
622.heading: Document

623.sourceSearchName: video mediated collaboration video mediated collaboration
623.title: Video-Mediated Collaboration
623.heading: Video-Mediated Collaboration
623.content:
Video-mediated collaboration shares live imagery of a participant or task environment with a remote collaborator. AR can register virtual objects, marks, or pointing cues with the video so guidance refers directly to visible physical features.

A fixed camera, participant-held camera, or head-mounted view provides different context and control. Delay, limited field of view, viewpoint choice, and alignment of annotations affect how well the remote user can understand the scene.

624.sourceSearchName: video mediated collaboration video mediated collaboration
624.title: Video-Mediated Collaboration
624.heading: References

625.sourceSearchName: video story clustering video story clustering
625.title: Video Story Clustering
625.heading: Document

626.sourceSearchName: video story clustering video story clustering
626.title: Video Story Clustering
626.heading: Video Story Clustering
626.content:
Video story clustering first segments a stream into coherent story units and then groups units describing the same event or topic. Visual shots, speech transcripts, audio cues, captions, and temporal proximity provide complementary evidence.

Temporal continuity aids segmentation, while multimodal similarity aids cross-story grouping. Repetition and evolving events complicate the boundary between a continuation of one story and a newly emerging but related topic.

632.sourceSearchName: video see through display video see through display
632.title: Video See-Through Display
632.heading: Video See-Through Display
632.content:
A video see-through display captures the physical world with a camera and electronically composites that image with generated imagery. The user views the completed image on an otherwise conventional display rather than looking directly through an optical combiner.

The digital pipeline gives the renderer control over both real and virtual pixels, which supports pixel-level registration, occlusion, and common image processing. Camera and display delay, limited resolution, distortion, and a viewpoint offset between camera and eye can weaken the experience.

633.title: Video See-Through Display

635.title: Video Game
635.heading: Video Game
635.content:
A video game is a [[Game]] mediated by a computer. Software implements the rules, maintains state, presents the game world, accepts player actions, and calculates their consequences.

Computer mediation enables rapid bookkeeping, hidden information, complex simulations, artificial opponents, networked play, and audiovisual feedback. It also means that permitted actions are limited to what the software and interface implement.

638.title: Video Avatar
638.heading: Video Avatar
638.content:
A video avatar represents a remote participant with captured image content placed inside a shared virtual or augmented space. The representation may be a textured plane, a segmented body image, or video mapped onto reconstructed geometry.

Unlike a fully synthetic avatar, it preserves real appearance and nonverbal behavior from the camera. Its viewpoint, scale, segmentation, and placement determine whether it conveys presence without conflicting with the surrounding scene.

641.title: Vertical Slice
641.heading: Vertical Slice
641.content:
A vertical slice is a polished sample in which representative layers of a game work together, from interface and art through gameplay systems and supporting technology. It demonstrates how the finished experience may appear to stakeholders.

Unlike a fast [[Prototype]], it requires polish and broad integration, so it is expensive and can distract from unresolved core design questions. Completing one also does not make the rest of an innovative game a merely linear content-production task.

A smaller [[Tracer Bullet]] can reduce end-to-end technical uncertainty before this level of polish is justified. Both forms gain their value from crossing component boundaries, not from demonstrating isolated task completion.

644.title: VFR Cross-Country Planning Sequence
644.heading: VFR Cross-Country Planning Sequence
644.content: A VFR cross-country plan proceeds from weather and aerodrome information to route selection, headings, performance, time, fuel, loading, frequencies, and plan filing. The order matters because later values depend on earlier choices such as altitude, true airspeed, wind, and alternates. Rechecking the complete plan exposes inconsistencies before they become in-flight workload.

645.title: VFR Cross-Country Planning Sequence

646.content:

Tags: [[Cloud Scalability and Resilience Patterns]]

647.title: Vertical Scaling
647.heading: Vertical Scaling
647.content: Vertical scaling increases or decreases the capacity of one running system by changing resources such as CPU, memory, or storage. A cloud host can move an application to a larger service tier without changing how many instances exist. This can relieve a bottleneck quickly, but one instance retains an upper size limit and may remain a single failure point.

650.title: Vertical Scalability
650.heading: Vertical Scalability
650.content:
Vertical scalability changes the capacity of an individual resource by making it more powerful, such as by increasing its memory or processing capability. The service continues to rely on fewer larger instances rather than adding more peers.

This contrasts with [[Horizontal Scalability]], which changes the number of resource instances. The two approaches have different operational limits, and the book defines cloud elasticity specifically through horizontal scaling out and in.

652.sourceSearchName: vertical line test vertical line test
652.title: Vertical Line Test
652.heading: Document

653.sourceSearchName: vertical line test vertical line test
653.title: Vertical Line Test
653.heading: Vertical Line Test
653.content: A plane graph represents $y$ as a [[Function]] of $x$ exactly when every vertical line intersects the graph at most once. A second intersection would assign two outputs to the same input. The test concerns the orientation of the graph, so a relation that fails it may still express $x$ as a function of $y$.

654.sourceSearchName: vertical line test vertical line test
654.title: Vertical Line Test
654.heading: References

655.sourceSearchName: vertical business process vertical business process
655.title: Vertical Business Process
655.heading: Document

656.sourceSearchName: vertical business process vertical business process
656.title: Vertical Business Process
656.heading: Vertical Business Process
656.content:
A vertical business process directly participates in the distinctive business model of an industry or organization. Its workflow helps produce the product or service by which the organization creates value.

Because a vertical process is closely tied to competitive practice and internal stakeholders, it can be harder to standardize or outsource than a [[Horizontal Business Process]]. A cloud implementation must preserve the domain-specific rules and interfaces that make it part of the business.

657.sourceSearchName: vertical business process vertical business process
657.title: Vertical Business Process
657.heading: References

658.sourceSearchName: vertical blank interval vertical blank interval
658.title: Vertical Blank Interval
658.heading: Document

659.sourceSearchName: vertical blank interval vertical blank interval
659.title: Vertical Blank Interval
659.heading: Vertical Blank Interval
659.content:
The vertical blank interval is the short period after a display finishes one image and before it begins scanning the next. Historically it reflected the return of a CRT electron beam to the top of the screen.

Presenting a completed back buffer during this interval prevents [[Screen Tearing]]. Modern display technology differs from CRT hardware, but vertical synchronization preserves the same timing contract between rendering and presentation.

660.sourceSearchName: vertical blank interval vertical blank interval
660.title: Vertical Blank Interval
660.heading: References

662.title: Vertical Asymptote
662.heading: Vertical Asymptote
662.content: The line $x=a$ is a vertical asymptote when a function becomes unbounded as $x$ approaches $a$ from at least one side. In a [[Rational Function]], an uncancelled denominator zero commonly creates this behavior. Left- and right-hand limits may approach different infinities, so each direction must be examined separately.

665.title: Vertical Angles
665.heading: Vertical Angles
665.content: Vertical angles are the opposite angles formed when two lines intersect. Each angle forms a linear pair with the same adjacent angle, so both are supplements of that shared angle and are therefore equal. This basic equality supports angle chasing in constructions involving intersecting lines and polygons.

668.title: Vertex
668.heading: Vertex
668.content:
A vertex is one of the objects represented in a [[Graph]]. It is also called a node. What it stands for depends on the model: a landmass, person, web page, task, or fragment of a biological sequence can all become vertices.

An [[Edge]] records a selected relationship between two vertices. The number of edges adjacent to a vertex is its [[Vertex Degree]], while direction and weight can add further meaning to the connection.

670.sourceSearchName: vertex cut partitioning vertex cut partitioning
670.title: Vertex-Cut Partitioning
670.heading: Document

671.sourceSearchName: vertex cut partitioning vertex cut partitioning
671.title: Vertex-Cut Partitioning
671.heading: Vertex-Cut Partitioning
671.content:
Vertex-cut partitioning assigns edges to partitions and allows a vertex to appear as replicas wherever its incident edges are stored. High-degree vertices can therefore have their work distributed across several machines.

Better edge balance comes at the cost of synchronizing replicated vertex state, so the method favors graphs where degree skew makes ordinary edge cuts expensive.

672.sourceSearchName: vertex cut partitioning vertex cut partitioning
672.title: Vertex-Cut Partitioning
672.heading: References

673.sourceSearchName: vertex centric graph processing vertex centric graph processing
673.title: Vertex-Centric Graph Processing
673.heading: Document

674.sourceSearchName: vertex centric graph processing vertex centric graph processing
674.title: Vertex-Centric Graph Processing
674.heading: Vertex-Centric Graph Processing
674.content:
Vertex-centric graph processing expresses an algorithm as the behavior of one vertex receiving information, updating local state, and communicating with neighbors. A framework applies this function across the graph in parallel.

The abstraction is concise for PageRank, shortest paths, and propagation, but it can hide expensive communication and uneven work caused by high-degree vertices.

675.sourceSearchName: vertex centric graph processing vertex centric graph processing
675.title: Vertex-Centric Graph Processing
675.heading: References

677.title: Vertex Skinning
677.heading: Vertex Skinning
677.content:
Vertex skinning deforms a mesh by transforming each vertex with one or more animated bone matrices and blending the results. The vertex stores bone indices and corresponding [[Skin Weight|weights]].

Performing the calculation in a [[Vertex Shader]] lets the GPU animate many vertices in parallel. Normals must be transformed consistently with positions so lighting follows the deformed surface.

680.title: Vertex Shader
680.heading: Vertex Shader
680.content:
A vertex shader is a GPU program executed for each submitted vertex. It reads attributes and uniform data, performs transformations or deformation, and must output the vertex position in clip space.

Additional outputs such as texture coordinates, normals, or world positions are interpolated across the primitive for the [[Fragment Shader]]. The shader's declared inputs must match the mesh's [[Vertex Attribute Layout]].

683.title: Vertex Degree
683.heading: Vertex Degree
683.content:
The degree of a vertex is the number of edges adjacent to it. It summarizes how many direct connections a [[Vertex]] has within a [[Graph]].

Degree can determine whether particular routes are possible. In the Königsberg bridge graph, more than two vertices had odd degree, preventing an [[Eulerian Path]]. It also constrains coloring: the largest vertex degree helps bound the number of colors required for [[Edge Coloring]].

685.sourceSearchName: vertex colors in blender vertex colors in blender
685.title: Vertex Colors in Blender
685.heading: Document

686.sourceSearchName: vertex colors in blender vertex colors in blender
686.title: Vertex Colors in Blender
686.heading: Vertex Colors in Blender
686.content:
Vertex colors store color values on mesh vertices. A face whose vertices have different values displays an interpolated gradient, making smooth color transitions possible without dividing the mesh into sharply separated material slots.

Vertex Paint mode provides brush-based editing so colors need not be entered one vertex at a time. The data applies only to meshes and must be connected appropriately to the material if it is to appear in rendered output.

687.sourceSearchName: vertex colors in blender vertex colors in blender
687.title: Vertex Colors in Blender
687.heading: References

688.sourceSearchName: vertex attribute layout vertex attribute layout
688.title: Vertex Attribute Layout
688.heading: Document

689.sourceSearchName: vertex attribute layout vertex attribute layout
689.title: Vertex Attribute Layout
689.heading: Vertex Attribute Layout
689.content:
A vertex attribute layout defines how bytes in a [[GPU Vertex Buffer]] map to shader inputs. Each attribute specifies a component count, numeric type, stride between vertices, and offset within one vertex record.

The layout must agree with both the C++ vertex structure and the [[Vertex Shader]]. A mismatched stride or offset causes the GPU to read unrelated bytes as positions, normals, texture coordinates, or other values.

690.sourceSearchName: vertex attribute layout vertex attribute layout
690.title: Vertex Attribute Layout
690.heading: References

691.sourceSearchName: vertex array object vertex array object
691.title: Vertex Array Object
691.heading: Document

692.sourceSearchName: vertex array object vertex array object
692.title: Vertex Array Object
692.heading: Vertex Array Object
692.content:
A vertex array object records the OpenGL bindings and attribute declarations needed to interpret a mesh's vertex and index buffers. Binding it restores the association between buffers and shader input locations for a draw.

The object does not replace the buffer data; it captures the configuration that explains that data. This reduces repeated state setup and keeps each mesh's [[Vertex Attribute Layout]] together.

693.sourceSearchName: vertex array object vertex array object
693.title: Vertex Array Object
693.heading: References

695.title: Vertex Coloring
695.heading: Vertex Coloring
695.content:
Vertex coloring assigns colors to the vertices of a [[Graph]] so that vertices joined by an edge never share a color. The colors represent categories or resources that must differ across every direct connection.

It is one form of [[Graph Coloring]]. The related [[Edge Coloring]] problem places the constraint on edges meeting at the same vertex instead of on adjacent vertices themselves.

698.title: Verification versus Validation in Thermal Modeling
698.heading: Verification versus Validation in Thermal Modeling
698.content:
Verification asks whether the mathematical model was implemented and solved correctly. Equation checks, conservation checks, solver convergence, and discretization studies address mistakes or numerical error between the intended equations and the computed answer.

Validation asks whether those equations and assumptions represent the physical system well enough for the intended decision. Analytical benchmarks and experiments such as [[Comparing Thermal Simulation with Infrared Measurements|thermal imaging]] supply independent evidence; a converged solution can still fail validation.
links: Comparing Thermal Simulation with Infrared Measurements

701.title: Vergence
701.heading: Vergence
701.content:
Vergence is the rotation of the eyes that allows their images to fuse at different viewing distances. The eyes converge for near objects and diverge for farther objects, and muscular feedback from this rotation acts as a [[Depth Cue]].

In natural viewing, vergence and [[Accommodation]] generally agree about distance. A stereoscopic display can draw images that drive vergence toward a virtual depth even though the physical screen keeps accommodation fixed at another depth. This mismatch is an important limit on visual [[Display Fidelity]] and can contribute to discomfort.

704.title: Verb Relationship
704.heading: Verb Relationship
704.content:
A verb relationship exists when two [[Game Verb|game verbs]] affect how one another can be used. Moving can determine where a shot is aimed, for example, while dodging may place the player where firing is temporarily unsafe.

Related verbs create choices that neither verb would produce alone. Their coordination can be introduced simply and then developed into more demanding combinations, allowing skill and understanding to grow without continually adding new controls.

707.title: Verb Development
707.heading: Verb Development
707.content:
Verb development is the process of deepening the player's relationship with a [[Game Verb]]. A developed verb gains new responsibilities, participates in more relationships, and must be applied in increasingly nuanced situations.

Development does not require adding more controls. Designers can vary timing, combine existing verbs, or introduce objects that change the consequences of an established action. This preserves focus while expanding the [[Possibility Space]].

709.sourceSearchName: vendor lock in vendor lock in
709.title: Vendor Lock-In
709.heading: Document

710.sourceSearchName: vendor lock in vendor lock in
710.title: Vendor Lock-In
710.heading: Vendor Lock-In
710.content:
Vendor lock-in is the dependency that makes leaving a provider costly or operationally difficult. It can arise from provider-specific application frameworks, data formats, interfaces, skills, contracts, integration, and the work required to recreate an environment elsewhere.

The risk can be reduced through open formats, independent backups, portable application and data architecture, and tested alternatives. Complete avoidance may sacrifice valuable provider capabilities, so the dependency should be understood and accepted deliberately.

711.sourceSearchName: vendor lock in vendor lock in
711.title: Vendor Lock-In
711.heading: References

713.title: Velocity
713.heading: Velocity
713.content:
Velocity is the amount of relatively estimated work a team completes within a Sprint. An average over several Sprints helps forecast how much similarly estimated backlog may fit into a future release.

Velocity is evidence for the team's own planning, not a commitment or a performance ranking. Comparing it across teams or rewarding higher numbers encourages estimate inflation rather than greater delivered value.

715.sourceSearchName: velocity verlet integration velocity verlet integration
715.title: Velocity Verlet Integration
715.heading: Document

716.sourceSearchName: velocity verlet integration velocity verlet integration
716.title: Velocity Verlet Integration
716.heading: Velocity Verlet Integration
716.content:
Velocity Verlet integration advances position using current velocity and acceleration, then updates velocity using acceleration information across the interval. It offers better stability and energy behavior than basic [[Euler Integration]] for many physical simulations.

Like other numerical integration methods, it depends on a controlled time step. It approximates continuous motion through successive discrete updates rather than producing an exact trajectory.

717.sourceSearchName: velocity verlet integration velocity verlet integration
717.title: Velocity Verlet Integration
717.heading: References

719.title: Velocity Potential
719.heading: Velocity Potential
719.content:
A velocity potential is a scalar field whose spatial gradient gives the velocity components of an irrotational flow. Solving for one nodal scalar can therefore replace direct solution of multiple velocity components.

In an incompressible source-free region, the potential satisfies Laplace's equation. Finite element differentiation of the interpolated potential recovers element velocities after the nodal values are known.

722.title: Velocity and Acceleration Unit Conversion
722.heading: Velocity and Acceleration Unit Conversion
722.content: Velocity has length per time, while acceleration has length per time squared. The book's examples convert ft/s to m/s and ft/s² to m/s² with the same $0.3048\ \mathrm{m/ft}$ factor because seconds remain unchanged in both cases. If the time unit also changed, the denominator would have to be converted once for velocity but twice for acceleration. The unit expression, not the quantity's label alone, determines the factor chain. See [[Compound Rate Unit Conversion]] and [[Dimensional Homogeneity in Equations]].

725.title: Vehicular Cloud
725.heading: Vehicular Cloud
725.content:
A vehicular cloud pools computing, storage, sensing, and communication resources contributed by vehicles. A coordinating system presents these changing resources as services for participating applications.

Vehicle mobility makes membership, connectivity, incentives, privacy, and reliability more variable than in a conventional fixed data center.

727.sourceSearchName: vehicular resource sharing vehicular resource sharing
727.title: Vehicular Resource Sharing
727.heading: Document

728.sourceSearchName: vehicular resource sharing vehicular resource sharing
728.title: Vehicular Resource Sharing
728.heading: Vehicular Resource Sharing
728.content:
Vehicular resource sharing lets owners contribute otherwise idle processor, storage, network, or sensing capacity to a pooled service. Compensation may include parking, charging, payment, or access to other services.

A workable mechanism must measure contribution, enforce limits, protect owner data, account for wear and energy, and remain safe for the vehicle's primary functions.

729.sourceSearchName: vehicular resource sharing vehicular resource sharing
729.title: Vehicular Resource Sharing
729.heading: References

730.sourceSearchName: vehicular cloud taxonomy vehicular cloud taxonomy
730.title: Vehicular Cloud Taxonomy
730.heading: Document

731.sourceSearchName: vehicular cloud taxonomy vehicular cloud taxonomy
731.title: Vehicular Cloud Taxonomy
731.heading: Vehicular Cloud Taxonomy
731.content:
A vehicular cloud taxonomy classifies deployments by factors such as whether vehicles are moving or parked, who controls the cloud, how participants connect, and what services they provide. The categories expose different assumptions about stability and available infrastructure.

Classifying a proposal prevents performance claims from a long-residency wired setting from being applied uncritically to a short-lived wireless one.

732.sourceSearchName: vehicular cloud taxonomy vehicular cloud taxonomy
732.title: Vehicular Cloud Taxonomy
732.heading: References

733.sourceSearchName: vehicle based data center vehicle based data center
733.title: Vehicle-Based Data Center
733.heading: Document

734.sourceSearchName: vehicle based data center vehicle based data center
734.title: Vehicle-Based Data Center
734.heading: Vehicle-Based Data Center
734.content:
A vehicle-based data center provides conventional computing and storage services from coordinated resources hosted in vehicles. Unlike a fixed facility, its capacity changes as participants arrive and leave.

Sufficient residency time and interconnection bandwidth are the source's key conditions for supporting big-data applications. Scheduling, replication, and migration translate those physical conditions into usable service continuity.

735.sourceSearchName: vehicle based data center vehicle based data center
735.title: Vehicle-Based Data Center
735.heading: References

736.sourceSearchName: vehicular cloud network vehicular cloud network
736.title: Vehicular Cloud Network
736.heading: Document

737.sourceSearchName: vehicular cloud network vehicular cloud network
737.title: Vehicular Cloud Network
737.heading: Vehicular Cloud Network
737.content:
A vehicular cloud network interconnects participating vehicles with coordinators, storage, and external services. Wireless links support mobility but can be bandwidth-constrained and variable; wired parking-lot connections can provide stable high throughput.

Topology and bandwidth determine whether the cloud can move virtual-machine state and big datasets quickly enough for useful computation.

740.title: Vector
740.heading: Vector
740.content:
A vector is an ordered row or column of values. It is a special case of a [[Matrix]] and can represent a state, a set of coordinates, or a collection of related measurements.

In PageRank, the [[PageRank Vector]] contains one relative-importance value for every web page. Repeated [[Vector-Matrix Multiplication]] updates those values until they converge to an [[Eigenvector]] of the Google matrix.

A row vector is a $1\times n$ matrix and a column vector is an $n\times1$ matrix. Beyond coordinates, a vector is any element of a [[Vector Space]], where [[Vector Addition]] and [[Scalar Multiplication of a Vector]] obey the vector-space axioms.

The source collects all observed outcomes into one column vector and all unknown linear-model parameters into another. Vector notation replaces a separate scalar equation for every experimental unit with a single matrix equation that is easier to manipulate and implement in R.

742.sourceSearchName: vehicle residency time vehicle residency time
742.title: Vehicle Residency Time
742.heading: Document

743.sourceSearchName: vehicle residency time vehicle residency time
743.title: Vehicle Residency Time
743.heading: Vehicle Residency Time
743.content:
Vehicle residency time is the duration a vehicle remains available to a vehicular cloud. A workload must either finish within that interval or move and replicate its state before departure.

Longer and more predictable residence improves capacity planning and makes virtual-machine setup worthwhile; uncertain short stays raise churn and recovery overhead.

744.sourceSearchName: vehicle residency time vehicle residency time
744.title: Vehicle Residency Time
744.heading: References

745.sourceSearchName: vector matrix multiplication vector matrix multiplication
745.title: Vector-Matrix Multiplication
745.heading: Document

746.sourceSearchName: vector matrix multiplication vector matrix multiplication
746.title: Vector-Matrix Multiplication
746.heading: Vector-Matrix Multiplication
746.content:
Vector-matrix multiplication multiplies each element of a row [[Vector]] by the corresponding element of a matrix column and sums the products. Repeating this for every column produces a new vector.

In the [[Power Method]], the current vector is repeatedly multiplied by the same matrix. PageRank uses this operation to redistribute every page's importance through the graph in each iteration.

747.sourceSearchName: vector matrix multiplication vector matrix multiplication
747.title: Vector-Matrix Multiplication
747.heading: References

749.title: Vector Subspace
749.heading: Vector Subspace
749.content:
A vector subspace is a nonempty subset of a [[Vector Space]] that remains a vector space under the inherited operations.

It is enough to check closure under [[Vector Addition]] and [[Scalar Multiplication of a Vector]]. Null spaces, column spaces, and [[Eigenspace|eigenspaces]] are important examples.

752.title: Vector Space
752.heading: Vector Space
752.content:
A vector space is a nonempty set whose elements can be added and multiplied by scalars while satisfying closure, associativity, commutativity of addition, distributive laws, and identity and inverse axioms.

The familiar space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is one example, but vectors may also be polynomials or functions. [[Basis]] and dimension describe the independent directions available in the space.

755.title: Vector Reflection
755.heading: Vector Reflection
755.content:
Vector reflection produces the direction obtained when an incoming vector bounces across a surface normal. It reverses the component pointing into the surface while preserving the component parallel to it.

With a normalized normal, the reflected vector can be derived from the incoming vector and their [[Dot Product]]. The operation supports effects such as ricochets, mirrored directions, and idealized light reflection.

758.title: Vector Projection
758.heading: Vector Projection
758.content:
Vector projection extracts the part of one vector that lies along another direction. With a normalized basis direction, the [[Dot Product]] gives the signed scalar amount along that direction, and multiplying the basis by that amount produces the projected vector.

Projection is useful for resolving motion or force along an axis, surface, or line. The remaining perpendicular component can be found by subtracting the projection from the original vector.

761.title: Vector Normalization
761.heading: Vector Normalization
761.content:
Vector normalization divides a nonzero vector by its magnitude to produce a unit vector pointing in the same direction. The normalized result has length one, so direction is separated from distance or speed.

Unit directions simplify lighting, movement, and angle calculations. A zero vector cannot be normalized because it has no direction and would require division by zero.

764.title: Vector Norm
764.heading: Vector Norm
764.content:
A vector norm measures vector magnitude. Common forms include the $1$-norm $\sum_i|x_i|$, Euclidean norm $(\sum_i x_i^2)^{1/2}$, and infinity norm $\max_i|x_i|$.

Norms provide distances between approximations, residual sizes, and stopping criteria for iterative methods. Different norms emphasize total, geometric, or worst-component error.

Game geometry most often uses the Euclidean norm for displacement and distance. When only a comparison is needed, [[Squared Vector Length]] avoids the square root while preserving which vector is longer.

766.sourceSearchName: vector in game programming vector in game programming
766.title: Vector in Game Programming
766.heading: Document

767.sourceSearchName: vector in game programming vector in game programming
767.title: Vector in Game Programming
767.heading: Vector in Game Programming
767.content:
A vector in game programming is an ordered set of components used to represent spatial quantities such as position, displacement, direction, velocity, and acceleration. Whether a value behaves as a point or a direction depends on its meaning and the operation being performed.

Vectors support the same reusable geometric operations across rendering, physics, cameras, audio, and artificial intelligence. Their components make spatial relationships explicit enough to calculate.

768.title: Vector in Game Programming
